summary: In this excerpt from Book 15, part 140 of a fiction work, Ray talks with Amah, who leads a children's Trust, and Emma about the Whiston Trust's facilities. Amah explains that the Trust takes in orphans and teaches them skills, customs and education so they can assimilate into the colony on New Holyoke, with staff at Blackheath Grange continuing the work. Ray, who expressed concern about the children's emotional well-being, offers polite pleasantries while privately doubting whether the arrangement is ideal or just the best of poor options.
one_line: Ray speaks with Amah about how the Whiston Trust educates orphans for life on the colony of New Holyoke.
key_facts: Amah says the children in the Trust have great potential and that the Trust looks for that potential and helps them develop it.
Amah says the Trust tries to give the children the facsimile of family as they go along.
Ray says losing your parents is a pretty big blow to try to bounce back from.
Amah says some children have been without parents, comforts, and love for several years, and those cases take longer for the colony to embrace them.
Amah says the children need to learn to assimilate, avoid social blunders, and contribute to a society that is radically different from the one they left behind.
Amah says the Trust has only a short time to introduce the children to the type of lives they will lead on New Holyoke.
Amah says Blackheath Grange has better facilities and a large staff to continue the process once the children are in the world.
Amah says that in return for education and skills, the children receive love, friendship, support, and an extended family.
Emma would like to show Ray the city, according to Amah, and Amah offers true Whiston hospitality to erase the harm.
Ray says he did not intend to sound critical when he questioned the children's emotional well-being.
Ray is privately unsure whether he agrees in principle with the Trust's approach or whether it is just the best of a poor lot of options.
Ray says he understands and exchanges what he assumes are more or less appropriate pleasantries.
Amah describes the curriculum as advanced for some children, while others lag significantly behind their expected educational level.
The excerpt ends with Ray relieved that he is not being cackled after for threatening the tranquility and security of the Whiston.
